articles.title: Kansas City building dating to 1874 faced emergency demolition after part of its roof collapsed; a developer stepped in, and the former fur shop is now being turned into a restaurant and apartments
articles.summary: A historic building in Kansas City, dating back to 1874, has been saved from demolition after part of its roof collapsed and city inspectors ordered its
articles.body: A historic building in Kansas City, dating back to 1874, has been saved from demolition after part of its roof collapsed and city inspectors ordered its emergency removal. The former Seiden's Furs building at 935 Broadway is widely considered the oldest surviving commercial building in downtown Kansas City's Downtown Loop. It is now being renovated into a Midwestern restaurant called Loretta Jean's, with apartments planned for the upper floors. The rescue was led by local developer Chris Sally, who stepped in to buy the property in October 2023, shortly after city officials issued an emergency demolition order. This was reported by the Kansas City Business Journal and Flatland KC. The project required major cleaning and structural repairs. Workers removed more than 20 dumpsters of abandoned stock and rubbish that had built up over several decades. They also pumped out dangerous standing water that had collected in the basement.Collapse and municipal actionThe building began falling into serious disrepair in July 2021, when heavy rainfall caused a large section of its roof to collapse. After the damage, city building inspectors officially declared the property dangerous. This led to several years of uncertainty about whether the historic building would survive. According to records cited by the non-profit preservation group Preserve Missouri, early engineering estimates placed the cost of necessary repairs at around $2.1 million (£1.6 million). There are still differences in reports about the building's total interior size. An early report by Flatland KC described it as covering 14,000 square feet. However, a later report published by The KC Pulse listed its size as 7,500 square feet. Jackson County's property tax records valued the building at $316,135 in 2019, before the roof collapsed. Before Sally agreed to buy the property, several other ideas were suggested to save it. Local reports by Flatland KC mentioned plans ranging from an underground speakeasy bar to workspaces for artists. One proposal came from artist Peregrine Honig, who wanted to create affordable artist studios with monthly rents of $200 to $400.Retail history from 1874 to 2006Built 152 years ago, the building first opened as the Brackett Brothers Drug Store. It later became a fur shop in 1935, according to coverage by the Kansas City Star. The business, known as Seiden's Furs, operated at the Broadway location for many years. However, historical records differ slightly about when it finally closed. The Kansas City Star reported that the fur shop remained open until 2006, while historical records kept by Preserve Missouri state that it closed in 2007. Sally's redevelopment plans aim to keep several features from the building's retail history. According to reports by Axios and the Kansas City Star, the new restaurant will include a preserved walk-in fur storage vault, an old metal safe used to store money, vintage advertising posters, and original fashion mannequins. These items will help maintain the building's historic character. Restoration workers have installed a completely new roof, repaired the mortar between the exterior bricks, and returned the second-floor windows to their original sizes, according to project updates from The KC Pulse.Restaurant plans and preservation honorsThe renovated building will house Loretta Jean's, a restaurant being developed by chef Rick Mullins and Candice Moore. According to details reported by Axios, the plans also include a separate private dining area or basement bar called Josephine's. The entire upper floor will be converted into residential apartments. The project received recognition from regional historic preservation groups even before the restaurant officially opened. According to Kansas City Magazine, the redevelopment received a 2025 Historic Kansas City Preservation Award for Neighborhood Stabilization. The publication reported that Loretta Jean's is expected to open in autumn 2026.Broader urban preservation effortsThe rescue of the Seiden's Furs building is part of a growing effort to save old and damaged historic buildings across downtown Kansas City. According to reporting by Flatland KC, a similar project saved the former Cosby Hotel, a building dating back to 1881. The property was close to demolition before private developers stepped in and turned it into commercial offices and dining space. The problem of neglected historic buildings has also led to action from local government officials and community leaders. Reporting by public broadcaster KCUR confirms that Kansas City Mayor Quinton Lucas recently introduced three city ordinances aimed at stopping historic buildings from falling into serious disrepair. At the same time, the non-profit organisation Historic KC published its first Most Endangered Places list in five years. The list aims to draw public attention to historic buildings and architecture across the region, according to additional reporting by KCUR.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2001, two Tofino residents spent 28 days in an 800-year-old cedar marked for removal; a steel brace eventually helped save the landmark tree
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of Herbie, the 800-year-old red cedar in Tofino, BC, and how two residents protested its removal, leading to innovative engineering solutions and a lasting environmental legacy.
articles.body: On Vancouver Island's west coast, a western red cedar known as the Eik Cedar became the focus of a protest in Tofino in 2001. The tree had been declared a danger because it was considered a potential hazard to nearby development. The Tofino Arts Council records that the cedar was already estimated to be about 700 years old when Norwegian settler John Eik claimed the property in 1896. Applying that historical estimate to 2026 would make the tree roughly 830 years old, although its age remains approximate.Weeks in the branchesTwo protesters climbed about 24 metres into the cedar's canopy and remained there for 28 days to prevent its removal. This duration is recorded in a local history of Tofino, which also describes the protest's national media attention. On May 14, 2001, Tofino council voted to defer the tree's removal for up to 45 days while the developer prepared a proposal for a support structure. The resolution required the design to be prepared and certified by a structural engineer. It also required the protesters to leave the tree and end their demonstrations before the arrangement could proceed.The council’s written resolution also set out how the arrangement would be maintained after construction. It required financial security equal to 120 per cent of the structural engineer’s estimated cost of the support system. The developer or a community group had to provide this security so the District could pay for maintenance and, if necessary, replacement. This mattered because the brace was not treated as a one time repair. Its future upkeep had to be backed by a funding arrangement rather than left to chance. Municipal staff were instructed to report on the developer’s progress at every council meeting. If the rezoning application did not advance with reasonable diligence, councillors retained the option of reconsidering the tree’s removal. The resolution also made clear that the protesters had to leave the site before the municipality acted on the proposed arrangement. Everyone had to leave the tree and remove their equipment and signs from municipal property, and demonstrations had to stop. These conditions show how the dispute moved from a direct protest into a formal municipal process. Keeping the cedar meant balancing public access, development plans, safety concerns and a funding arrangement for the structure’s future upkeep.A brace built to lastResidents formed the Tofino Natural Heritage Society to organise the campaign to save the cedar. The society hired a structural engineer to develop a support system that would address the safety concerns surrounding the tree. In summer 2002, engineers fitted the trunk with a specially designed metal girdle anchored into the bedrock. The structure allowed the cedar to remain standing while reducing the risk that had led to its proposed removal. A local history of Tofino documents the installation and describes the support system as a key part of the tree's preservation. The Eik Cedar protest became an example of direct action in tree protection. The protesters' occupation delayed the proposed removal, but the tree's long-term preservation required a local heritage society and a specially engineered support structure. More than two decades after its installation, the steel girdle remains part of the story of how the community helped save the cedar.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After Hurricane Sandy, scientists fenced deer out of damaged parts of New York’s Fire Island; 3 years later, fenced plots carried more plant cover than unfenced plots
articles.summary: A study reveals fenced areas on New York's Fire Island, after Hurricane Sandy, have significantly more plant cover than unfenced plots. The impact of deer on vegetation recovery examined three years post-storm.
articles.body: Barrier islands depend on dunes and vegetation to protect their interiors from waves and storm surge. When a powerful storm washes sand across the dunes, it can remove much of the plant cover that holds the landscape together. Fire Island, a barrier island off the south shore of Long Island, New York, offered scientists a chance to study how vegetation recovers after a major storm.After Hurricane Sandy struck on October 29, 2012, researchers examined damaged areas in the Otis Pike Fire Island High Dune Wilderness Area. The storm left nine overwash fans, where surge carried sand inland and removed much of the existing vegetation and foredunes. Before the hurricane, foredunes in the study area stood between 4 and 15 meters high. Sandy also opened a channel at Old Inlet, connecting the ocean and Great South Bay. The National Park Service says the breach has shifted over time but remained relatively stable since 2013. The park service's account of the Old Inlet breach explains how storms and moving sediment continue to reshape this part of the island.Deer grazing slowed vegetation recoveryThe researchers were interested in one possible obstacle to recovery: white-tailed deer. Deer are the main large herbivores on Fire Island, and they eat grasses and other plants. Their hooves can also damage vegetation and disturb sandy ground. Trail camera monitoring suggested that deer used the recovering overwash fans much more heavily than the wider wilderness area. The study estimated local use at an average of about 27 deer per hectare, compared with long-term area-wide estimates of 0.25 to 0.40 deer per hectare. This was a local estimate for the small study areas, not a count of the entire island's herd. The study in AoB Plants reports the method and comparison.Beachgrass was central to the recovery question. American beachgrass grows through the sand, sending out roots and shoots as more sand accumulates around its base. This growth traps additional sand and can gradually rebuild a dune. Other shrubs and herbs can then establish in the shelter behind it. If grazing or trampling limits the grass, the formation of new dunes may slow, leaving areas farther inland more exposed to future storms.How researchers tested the effects of deerThe researchers set up 61 permanent plots across the nine overwash fans in spring 2013. Some plots were surrounded by wire fences that deer could not enter, while nearby comparison plots remained open. The fences were about 1.5 meters high and were buried approximately 30 centimetres into the sand to prevent deer from getting underneath. Researchers surveyed the plots in September 2015 and 2016, recording plant cover and the number of species present.The results showed a clear difference in plant cover in both survey years. In 2015, vegetation covered an average of 58.2 per cent of fenced plots, compared with 33.2 per cent of unfenced plots. In 2016, cover reached 66 per cent inside the fences and 48.6 per cent outside. American beachgrass accounted for between 87 and 96 per cent of the vegetation cover. Researchers recorded 12 plant species across the permanent plots, although individual plots usually contained four or fewer species. Fenced plots also held a greater variety of species than open plots.A broader assessment recorded 29 plant species across the overwash fans during surveys in 2015 and 2016. That figure does not contradict the 12 species in the permanent plot study: the wider assessment covered more survey locations and methods than only the experimental plots. The report also examined sea beach amaranth, a federally threatened plant. Plants left outside protective fences were often heavily browsed by deer and died before producing seeds. The USGS report on deer browsing and vegetation recovery describes these wider findings.What the findings reveal about dune recoveryThe overall recovery was more complicated than a simple story of deer preventing plants from returning. Total vegetation cover across the overwash fans increased each year after Sandy, even as deer continued to use the area and a regional drought affected the island in 2016. Two overwash fans also experienced repeated coastal disturbances that complicated their recovery. The researchers could not separate the effects of deer eating plants from the damage caused by their trampling. Human activity could also disturb the sandy areas.The experiment therefore found that excluding deer was associated with greater plant cover and species richness in the monitored plots. It did not show that deer were the only factor shaping recovery, or that fencing alone could restore every damaged dune. Storms, shifting sand, drought and the gradual return of different plant species all influenced the landscape. For barrier islands such as Fire Island, the findings underline the role of vegetation in rebuilding dunes after severe storms and the importance of monitoring how those plants recover.You use AI every day. articles.title: An 868-acre California ranch was once slated for a golf course; in 2024, Midpen paid $4.8 million for 644 acres to keep it open beside Half Moon Bay forever
articles.summary: In a significant move to preserve the Johnston Ranch, Midpen paid $4.8 million for 644 acres, ensuring the land remains open space beside Half Moon Bay. This acquisition follows a decades-long effort to protect this site from development after voters rejected plans for a golf course in the 1990s.
articles.body: South of Half Moon Bay, California, Johnston Ranch covers 868 acres of coastal grasslands, agricultural fields and natural habitat. In the early 1990s, developers proposed turning the property into a golf course and luxury homes. San Mateo County voters rejected the proposal, opening the way for conservation groups to protect the land. In 2024, the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District, known as Midpen, completed the purchase of 644 acres of the ranch's uplands. The land became part of the adjacent Miramontes Ridge Open Space Preserve, while farmland remained under separate ownership. The official account of Johnston Ranch's preservation and transfer documents the property's history and current ownership.Midpen's board approved the $4.8 million purchase in November 2021, and the district began managing the uplands in December that year. However, the formal transfer of ownership from the Peninsula Open Space Trust, or POST, to Midpen was completed in June 2024. The distinction matters because management began more than two years before the ownership transfer was finalized.The vote that matteredThe property has a long history. It lies within the ancestral territory of the Ohlone peoples, including the Quiroste, who cultivated food and regularly burned grasslands before European settlement displaced them. In 1853, Scottish immigrant James Johnston purchased 1,162 acres of the Miramontes Rancho de San Benito along the southern part of Half Moon Bay. Johnston had arrived in California during the Gold Rush and later became a successful San Francisco businessman.In the early 1990s, the golf course and housing proposal faced strong local opposition. San Mateo County voters rejected it by 84%, creating an opportunity for POST, a private nonprofit land trust, to acquire and protect Johnston Ranch. POST purchased the property in two transactions, one in 1999 and another in 2001, for a combined $5.65 million. The two purchase dates and the total amount are confirmed in Midpen's historical account of the property. POST's longer-term plan was to find suitable stewards for the different parts of the property. That meant protecting the uplands as public open space while keeping the productive farmland available for continued agricultural use.Two owners, one ranchThe later ownership arrangement divided the ranch according to its conservation and agricultural uses. Midpen acquired the 644 acres of uplands for $4.8 million, using funds from Measure AA, which local voters approved in 2014. Grants totalling $700,000 from the Coastal Conservancy and the California State Parks Habitat Conservation Fund helped offset the acquisition cost. The district manages the uplands as part of its open space preserve system.POST retained the remaining 224 acres of prime agricultural land, where Giusti Farms has farmed for generations. POST holds an agricultural conservation easement over this farmland to prevent future development and ensure that it remains in production. The organisation has also expressed an intention to transfer ownership to the Giusti family in the future.What lives on the hillsMidpen characterises the uplands as rolling grassy slopes, coastal scrub and the Arroyo Leon Creek corridor. The rangelands that provide habitat for grasshopper and savanna sparrows, western meadowlarks, burrowing owls and American badgers are home to natural grasses such as California oatgrass, purple needlegrass and California meadow barley, as well as western rush. Cattle still graze the farm, but as a conservation strategy. Managed grazing can be beneficial to native grasslands that evolved with occasional disturbance, like those under a rangeland management plan Midpen wrote for a local rancher.People are part of the plan as well. When the transfer was announced, Midpen said it would conduct a public process on a possible loop trail near the Johnston House and connections to the adjacent Burleigh Murray Ranch State Park, while Half Moon Bay was preparing to plan a walking and cycling trail along Higgins Canyon Road to connect the house with downtown. And the house itself is owned by the city. The Johnston House Foundation says it is in the same place where it was erected in 1853, and it has arranged free, costumed docent visits on the third Saturday of each month from January through September in 2026.Johnston Ranch now has separate roles in conservation and agriculture. Midpen manages 644 acres of uplands as protected open space, while POST retains 224 acres of farmland under an agricultural conservation easement. The original $5.65 million was POST's combined purchase price for the larger property in 1999 and 2001. Midpen's later $4.8 million payment covered only the 644-acre upland section, not the entire ranch again and not an additional premium on the original purchase price. Grants helped offset that later acquisition, while Giusti Farms continued working the remaining agricultural land.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: The IShowSpeed livestreams, which have been entertaining fans for quite some time, provide more reasons than just fun and excitement to watch.
articles.body: The IShowSpeed livestreams, which have been entertaining fans for quite some time, provide more reasons than just fun and excitement to watch. The IShowSpeed partnership with Expedia created a paid clipping campaign that offered creators the opportunity to make money through the sharing of selected scenes from IShowSpeed’s livestream in October 2026. The clipping campaign was sponsored by the Reach agency and had an $8,000 budget, giving creators $1 for every 1,000 views. But there were certain requirements to be followed.IShowSpeed's Expedia clipping campaign offered $1 per 1,000 views to creatorsThe campaign was listed on Content Rewards on October 14, 2026, the same day IShowSpeed hosted his Expedia Unpack livestream. According to the campaign details checked on October 23, Reach was running the project with Expedia as its brand partner.Creators could earn between $10 and $500 for each approved clip. However, a video had to reach at least 10,000 views before it could qualify for payment. For example, a clip with 100,000 views could earn $100, while one with 250,000 views could earn $250. The maximum payment was capped at $500 per clip.The campaign had a total budget of $8,000, but only around $850 remained when it was checked on October 23. At that time, 143 clippers were already taking part.There was one important condition: creators could only use footage from the October 14 Expedia livestream. They could not take clips from IShowSpeed's other videos or streams.The videos also had to focus on IShowSpeed, with the yellow suitcase visible in the frame. Creators were encouraged to share his reactions to different travel destinations and the items revealed from the suitcase.Creators had to follow strict rules to earn money from IShowSpeed clipsThe campaign accepted videos posted on TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. Creators also had to include the hashtags #IShowSpeed and #Expedia and correctly name the destination shown in their clips.Reach had other rules for people who wanted to join. At least 50% of a creator's audience had to come from the US, Canada, Australia, the UK, or New Zealand. Their account also had to focus on streaming or travel content.The content that included AI clips, fake views, reposted content, and the video that displayed IShowSpeed or Expedia in any bad way was prohibited. The creators were also required to link their social media accounts to their Whop account and upload the link to the video within 30 minutes after its posting.On the other hand, it seems like IShowSpeed doesn't have his own constant clipping service on platforms like Content Rewards, Vyro, or Whop. The Expedia deal was a one-off partnership as opposed to the constant payment system for the clips.The campaign might have finished because of the end of its budget that remained quite low by October 23rd. However, it demonstrated the possibility for the brands to attract the audience via the clips from popular streamers' livestreams and earn some money as a video editor.You use AI every day. articles.title: November to be slightly warmer than usual, predicts IMD
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Nov is likely to be slightly warmer than usual, recording 'above normal' maximum (day) and minimum (night) temperatures over most parts of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Nov is likely to be slightly warmer than usual, recording 'above normal' maximum (day) and minimum (night) temperatures over most parts of the country, IMD said Saturday.The Met department also predicted that the country may get 'below normal' rainfall in most parts except for some areas in central, northwest and northeast India, where normal to 'above normal' rainfall is expected in Nov. 'Below normal' rainfall may be a concern for peninsular India as that part of the country usually gets good rain during Nov on account of the winter (northeast) monsoon.The prediction of normal to 'above normal' rainfall in some areas of central and northeast India assumes significance for Madhya Pradesh and adjoining areas of Maharashtra and Gujarat, east Uttar Pradesh and Bihar as it will help wheat crop in these rain-fed regions during the month.Meanwhile, the existing depression over southwest Bay of Bengal is likely to develop as a cyclonic storm on Sunday and cross south Andhra Pradesh and north Tamil Nadu coasts during the Monday evening-Tuesday morning period, bringing heavy rain to the coastal areas of both the states. Once the existing system develops into a cyclonic storm, it will be called 'Murasu'. 'Murasu' is a Tamil word which means a drum, particularly a traditional percussion instrument."Monthly rainfall for Nov over the south Peninsular India, consisting of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Karaikkal, coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema region, Kerala, Mahe and south interior Karnataka, is most likely to be 'below normal' (less than 77% of the long period average)," said IMD chief Mrutyunjay Mohapatra while releasing the monthly outlook for rainfall and temperature for Nov.The long period average of rainfall over south Peninsular India during Nov, based on data from 1971 to 2020, is 118.7 mm. In Oct, rainfall over the country (51.7 mm) was the sixth lowest since 2001 and 25th lowest since 1901, with a deficit of 31%. Rainfall over south Peninsular India (122.2 mm) was the sixth lowest since 2001.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Government extends Nilekani-led exam reforms panel tenure till Jan
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Centre has extended the tenure of the Nandan Nilekani-led task force on examination reforms till Jan 2027, with the prime minister's office
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Centre has extended the tenure of the Nandan Nilekani-led task force on examination reforms till Jan 2027, with the prime minister's office (PMO) seeking consultations with chief ministers and chief secretaries before the panel finalises its recommendations, TOI has learnt from govt officials. During consultations, some stakeholders and experts have also suggested a hybrid format for NEET-UG 2027, allowing time to expand infrastructure for a complete shift to computer-based testing (CBT) in 2028.A govt official said the PMO wants the task force, earlier expected to submit its report by Oct-end, to seek views from state leadership on challenges particular to different regions. The aim, the source said, is to better understand disparities in testing infrastructure, connectivity and administrative preparedness, and reflect these state-specific concerns in a more comprehensive examination reform roadmap.Another proposal likely to feature in the task force's recommendations is a nationwide network of CBT centres developed by Centre and state govts with private investment, sources said. Such a model could expand govt oversight of testing facilities while mobilising private capital to build infrastructure, particularly in districts that lack secure, adequately equipped centres. The funding, ownership and operating arrangements would need to be worked out. Such centres could support common security standards, reliable connectivity and better access for candidates outside metros.TOI had earlier reported that the task force is prioritising "debundling" examination responsibilities. Under the proposed restructuring, question-paper setting, conduct of exams, management of test centres and security would be assigned to separate agencies instead of being concentrated with a single operator.The objective is to create clearer lines of accountability and limit the risk of a lapse in one part of the examination process affecting the entire exercise. The approach would, however, require coordination between the agencies handling different stages.The panel is also considering exam centres in every district and a common calendar for National Testing Agency (NTA), Staff Selection Commission (SSC), Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS) and Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs). Coordinated schedules could help students and job applicants avoid exam-date clashes and allow testing infrastructure to be used more efficiently.The six-member task force was constituted in July following the NEET-UG 2026 controversy, which led to the cancellation of the original exam and a retest. It has held 18 internal meetings and around 40 consultations, in addition to seeking public suggestions.An Oct parliamentary committee report also recommended secure govt-controlled testing centres across districts and a phased transition to CBT for NEET-UG. The extension gives the task force more time to assess the feasibility of its proposals with states.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: From Mallikarjun Kharge's lawn, 250 opposition MPs 'impeach' CEC Gyanesh Kumar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: With Rahul Gandhi terming \"public impeachment\" and Sunday's Ramlila Maidan rally a \"dangerous political weapon\" targeting Modi-Shah-Gyanesh,
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With Rahul Gandhi terming "public impeachment" and Sunday's Ramlila Maidan rally a "dangerous political weapon" targeting Modi-Shah-Gyanesh, the INDIA bloc, in a symbolic move, Saturday passed a "resolution" to "impeach" CEC Gyanesh Kumar accusing it of colluding with the ruling BJP to compromise national election management. It also sought that Kumar be "tried for treason".Six "charges" of "premeditated attack on poll process" - as part of "criminal conspiracy" of BJP, PM Modi and Union minister Amit Shah - span questionable handling of poll rolls, "manipulated" SIR to delete 14 crore voters, illegal changes to Form 6 to block new voters, deletion of voters through software. CEC Kumar has also been accused of ignoring the two ECs in decision making.The "public impeachment" held in the lawns of the residence of Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge involved around 250 MPs from opposition. The venue was designed with Parliament chamber like decor, with former Speaker Meira Kumar in the high chair. LoP Rajya Sabha Kharge tabled the resolution while Rahul concluded the debate, before Meira Kumar put the resolution to vote that was passed by a voice vote. The slogan 'vote chor gaddi chhod' ended the assembly after three hours of debate.Setting the tone, Kharge said Modi has hatched conspiracies to retain power, which include engineering defections, splitting parties, electoral bonds, misuse of agencies, while adding the 2023 "immunity law" for the CEC is another such instrument.Underlining the need for "public impeachment", Kharge said RS and LS rejected the opposition notices for removal of Kumar. Rahul said 15% of 2024 voters have been deleted by SIR, which means the LS polls were illegal. "I can comfortably say Kumar will not survive as CEC. We have enough proof. If BJP keeps him after we reveal what we know, then the BJP game would be clear," he argued.Harendra Malik of SP said SIR has sought to target "PDA voters" of his party ahead of UP polls. Sagarika Ghose of TMC said 2026 Bengal polls were stolen after 29 lakh voters "vanished" under "Vanish Kumar's SIR". John Brittas (CPM), in a searing warning, said India should not be the Germany of 1930s, a parallel also drawn by Mamata TMC's Mahua Moitra.Those who spoke were Mehbooba Mufti (PDP), Arvind Sawant (Shiv Sena), Abhay Sinha (RJD), NK Premachandran (RSP), Sandosh Kumar (CPI), Rajeev Rai (SP), Durai Vaiko (MDMK), Kapil Sibal, Jose Mani (KCM), Devarajan (FB), ET Muhammed Basheer (IUML), Sudama Prasad (CPI-ML), Nasir Aslam (NC), Thol Thirumavalavan (VCK), Baidyanath Ram (JMM). Civil society luminaries like Yogendra Yadav, Nikhil Dey, Sharukh Alam advocate, Anjali Bharadwaj, Noor Shridhar provided incisive arguments and data to put the EC in the dock. Neha Bora of AISA and NSUI volunteer Ritu Barala also spoke.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: EKTA NAGAR, KEVADIA: PM Narendra Modi Saturday attacked opposition for abandoning its constitutional duty and instead resorting to politics of 'obstruction', driven by "despair and disappointment". Addressing the Rashtriya Ekta Diwas parade - organised annually on the birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel - Modi recalled how Sardar Patel and BR Ambedkar had, while framing the Constitution, clearly laid down duties and roles of govt and opposition."Opposition is exercising politics of 'obstruction', in complete disregard of constitutional boundaries and propriety," he added.Warning against divisive forces that have come out in the open after more than a decade of political frustration to plot conspiracies, pit citizens against one another, and weaponise social media to spread rumours and tarnish India's image, the PM urged citizens to recognise the patterns of such forces conducting secret foreign meetings, their external backing by anti-India elements, and their rhetoric echoing the nation's enemies. "We have ended Naxalism in remote areas, but the threat from ideological extremists (dimagi Naxals) is not yet over, and the country has to remain ever vigilant against such entities," he cautioned.Stressing that the grand mission of national unity and the journey toward a strong and capable India must continue regardless of difficulties, the PM outlined the next major national priorities of fully securing India's borders, putting an end to infiltration and resulting demographic changes, and advancing toward a secular civil code. Acknowledging that major resolutions and bold decisions will inevitably face roadblocks and storms, he declared that the nation will not be deterred from the unwavering resolves of 'Ek Bharat, Shreshtha Bharat' and a 'Viksit Bharat', working tirelessly with every breath and heartbeat toward the 2047 goal of a strong and capable India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Three falcons died after neighbouring building work disturbed a breeding aviary, and the Court of Appeal upheld £258,500 in damages despite rejecting the nuisance claim
articles.summary: In a Falcon breeding nuisance and negligence ruling, the Court of Appeal has upheld £258,500 in damages for a Cornwall falcon-breeding business, even
articles.body: In a Falcon breeding nuisance and negligence ruling, the Court of Appeal has upheld £258,500 in damages for a Cornwall falcon-breeding business, even though a majority of judges held the nuisance claim should have failed. Three falcons died after noise and visual disturbance from neighbouring scaffolding work, barn building and a broken-down digger during the 2022 breeding season. The award survived because two of the three judges found the neighbours also owed a duty of care in negligence. A sensitive business can therefore lose in nuisance yet still recover damages, where the neighbour knew the risk and could reasonably have avoided it.How a long-running neighbour dispute over a Cornwall falcon aviary reached the Court of AppealMartin and Scott Nicholas run Raptors of Penwith, which breeds gyr falcons, peregrine falcons and crosses between the two at Bosavern, near St Just. According to the judgment published by the British and Irish Legal Information Institute, the young birds are sent to Dubai for training, racing and onward sale. Martin has bred falcons on the site since 1995, and the current aviary was built from October 2018. Barnes Thomas and his company, Upper Cot Estate, became neighbours later, after buying adjoining farmland in 2020. Disputes over a septic tank, a drain and vehicle access to Thomas’s home soured relations. The High Court trial that followed ran for nine days and heard seventeen lay witnesses, two experts and 35 videos.What the trial judge found about the scaffolding, the barn building and the digger by the aviaryHis Honour Judge Russen, a King’s Counsel sitting as a High Court judge, preferred the brothers’ account on the key disputed facts. He found that Thomas knew from messages with Martin in December 2020 that noise and visual threats had to be avoided from March to May. Thomas had even told Martin he would not make noise in March. The judge found six of eight alleged incidents proved. They included scaffolding poles dropped on metal, leaving birds in distress on security camera footage on 27 March 2022, and groundworks for the barn that involved pecking out granite and made the aviary vibrate. The sixth was a broken-down digger left beside the aviary for three days from 7 April with its bucket raised, which Scott Nicholas said sent the birds into a frenzy. He also found that the scaffolding business was not an ordinary use of agricultural land. He dismissed the harassment claim, the counterclaim and the request for an injunction.Why two of the three appeal judges decided a sensitive falcon business could not rely on nuisanceThe appeal turned on a principle reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in the Tate Modern viewing gallery case, Fearn v Board of Trustees of the Tate Gallery, a person cannot increase a neighbour’s liability by putting land to a special use. International Comparative Legal Guides reported that Thomas and his company argued the falcon business fell into that category. Lord Justice Nugee agreed. He wrote that breeding falcons is a specialised use, and that a suitable location does not turn it into an ordinary one. He reasoned that a digger with a raised bucket would trouble no ordinary use of farmland, and that the noise complaints were pleaded as excessive for falcons rather than for ordinary occupiers. Lord Justice Moylan agreed that local character cannot convert a special use into an ordinary one. Lady Justice Whipple dissented. She held that the trial judge was entitled to find the use ordinary for its rural setting. She noted that stock breeding is common, and that expert evidence showed the birds tolerate regular noise but not sudden shocks during the breeding season.How the duty of care in negligence kept the damages alive and what the dissenting judge made of itNegligence rescued the award. Lord Justice Nugee held that neighbouring landowners can owe each other a duty to take reasonable care, and that Thomas, who had known of the risk for more than a year, could not simply disregard it. He said the digger could have been parked elsewhere and the building work timed differently. The trial judge had confined the duty to the period from 1 March to 5 May 2022. Lady Justice Whipple agreed on negligence in the alternative, saying she was struck by the injustice if the claim failed. Lord Justice Moylan dissented, warning that a duty based solely on the falcons’ sensitivity would undermine nuisance law and leave landowners unsure which ordinary activities were forbidden. The appeal was dismissed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Conservationists sought to release three lynx into England's Kielder Forest 1,300 years after the species vanished; High Court judge rejects group's regulatory challenge
articles.summary: Could one of Britain's lost wild predators return to its forests after more than 1,300 years?
articles.body: Could one of Britain's lost wild predators return to its forests after more than 1,300 years? A conservation group hoped to make that possible by bringing three Eurasian lynx to Northumberland's Kielder Forest for a monitored trial. The proposal aimed to explore whether the large wild cats could once again play a role in Britain's natural ecosystem, particularly by helping control deer populations. However, the plan faced a legal obstacle before the animals could be released, leading the organisation to challenge the decision of the country's wildlife regulator.In a judgment delivered on October 30, 2026, in R (Lynx UK Trust Community Interest Company) v Natural England ([2026] EWHC 2761 (Admin)), the High Court dismissed the conservation group's judicial review challenge. According to the primary judgment available through The National Archives, Ms Justice Obi ruled that permission to release lynx under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981 would not remove the separate legal requirements of the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976. The court found that the challenge to Natural England's refusal to assess the revised proposal had been brought too late and that, in any event, it would have failed on its merits.Why conservationists wanted to bring lynx backThe Lynx UK Trust Community Interest Company, a not-for-profit organisation promoting the conservation and reintroduction of lynx, had been exploring the possibility of bringing the species back to Britain for several years. Eurasian lynx are large wild cats that once lived in the country but have been extinct in the United Kingdom for more than 1,300 years. The organisation believed their return could support biodiversity and nature recovery by restoring the ecological role of a native apex predator. One expected benefit was their potential impact on deer populations, which can affect woodland regeneration and vegetation.The group first approached Natural England in 2015. In July 2017, it applied for permission to release six lynx into Kielder Forest as part of a five-year trial. However, Natural England's technical assessment found that the proposal did not meet the International Union for Conservation of Nature's guidelines. Concerns included insufficient ecological assessment, funding, organisational capacity, engagement with landowners and local communities, and monitoring arrangements. On November 30, 2018, the Secretary of State accepted Natural England's advice and refused the application.A smaller proposal involving three lynxThe conservation group later prepared a revised plan. Submitted in draft form on May 30, 2022, the new proposal involved releasing three lynx, two females and one male, into Kielder Forest for a three-year trial. The animals would be captured in Sweden and transported to Britain. They would initially stay in specially built enclosures for quarantine and acclimatisation before being gradually released into the forest. The plan also included tracking, veterinary supervision and arrangements to recapture the animals if necessary.The organisation said it would remain responsible for the health and welfare of the lynx and their offspring throughout the trial. However, another legal issue emerged. Lynx are included in the list of dangerous wild animals regulated under the Dangerous Wild Animals Act 1976. Natural England, the UK government’s advisory body on the natural environment, believed that even if the group received a release licence under the Wildlife and Countryside Act, it would still need to comply with the separate law governing the keeping of dangerous animals.On July 1, 2022, Natural England informed the organisation that it would not conduct a full assessment of the proposal because there was no foreseeable legal route for the release to proceed. It maintained this position in subsequent correspondence.What the conservation group argued in courtThe Lynx UK Trust challenged Natural England's decision, arguing that the two laws should be interpreted differently. Under the Wildlife and Countryside Act, releasing certain non-native animals into the wild requires a licence. The group argued that once such permission was granted, the Dangerous Wild Animals Act should no longer prevent the release.It also argued that the two laws were inconsistent and that the later Wildlife and Countryside Act should take precedence where the proposed release was authorised. Alternatively, the organisation maintained that Natural England should have assessed its application rather than refusing to consider it because of the separate legal requirements. Natural England and the government disagreed, arguing that the two laws served different purposes and could operate together.Why the High Court rejected the challengeMs Justice Obi ruled that the Dangerous Wild Animals Act continued to apply even after an animal was deliberately released. Under Section 7(1) of the Act, a person who stops possessing an animal remains legally responsible as its keeper until another person becomes its keeper. The judge explained that the law did not limit this continuing responsibility to situations involving an animal escaping or being lost. Therefore, a licence under the Wildlife and Countryside Act would not automatically end the obligations under the Dangerous Wild Animals Act.She also rejected the argument that the later legislation had implicitly overridden the earlier law. The two Acts dealt with different legal responsibilities and could operate alongside each other. The court refused permission on this ground, finding that the challenge was not brought promptly and was outside the time limit prescribed by CPR 54.5. The regulator had communicated its decision on July 1, 2022, while the judicial review proceedings were not filed until December 17, 2025. The judge also said Natural England was entitled to consider the legal obstacle and the public resources required for a full assessment.The claim was therefore dismissed. The ruling leaves the proposed lynx trial without the regulatory approval it sought, but it does not settle the wider scientific or environmental debate about whether the species should return to Britain's forests.You use AI every day. articles.title: Protests spread to Germany as hundreds of thousands march again in France
articles.summary: Cost-of-living protests that began in France have spread to Germany where demonstrations to coincide with Halloween were underway on Saturday, with tens of t...
articles.body:
Cost-of-living protests that began in France have spread to Germany where demonstrations to coincide with Halloween were underway on Saturday, with tens of thousands of people turning out across the country.

The new German youth-led movement dubbed "Gen Z has got this!" is protesting against the high cost of living, underfunded schools and universities, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service . Protests were planned in major cities including Berlin, Frankfurt, Cologne and Munich.

While the protest in the German capital appeared peaceful, water cannons and riot police were deployed in Cologne and Hamburg.

Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. "Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants," the police said in a statement.

In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers attacked. "There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this," the police said.

In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were being thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows had been smashed, prompting the closure of part of the Zeil shopping street. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop.

Organizers of 'Gen Z regelt' planned the large day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility.

"We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us," the movement states on its website. It adds that the intention is to protest peacefully and organizers instruct participants to keep their faces visible, even in Halloween costumes.

Extra German police officers have been deployed nationwide in preparation for the protest, and the luxury shops lining Berlin's upmarket Kurfürstendamm shopping street have boarded up their windows as a precautionary measure.

The German youth movement follows a broader wave of protests that have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which has been hit by rioting and looting and is now facing another weekend of rallies.

More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement were also underway in France on Saturday, in what has been billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24. Students and some unions are also expected to join.

French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people were protesting across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris. That is a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.

The ministry said that as of 6 p.m. local time, 296 people had been detained countrywide.

Warning of a "very high risk of public disorder," France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez announced this week that demonstrations would only be authorized outside town centers, with 70,000 extra law enforcement officers deployed nationwide.

The protest were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that "radical elements at the tail end of the processions" in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, "attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting."

The ministry said the police intervened and "thwarted" those attempts.

Jordan Bardella, the leader of France's far-right National Rally party, said on X that "anyone who sends an 'improvised incendiary device' to law enforcement must be very severely punished," adding that "perpetrators must rot in prison for very long years."

Police in Rennes in Brittany in northwest France, said that while the main march planned for Saturday "proceeded calmly along the planned route," several hundred violent individuals began attacking the police after the protest ended, throwing projectiles and setting off fires.

Violence has plagued the protests in recent week, with the ministry saying on Friday that as of October 29, at least 1,193 police officers had been injured since the start of the protests.

Halloween was adding a new complication to the protests, with Nuñez warning of separate calls for gatherings across France from 8 p.m. local time "by radical far-left groups and radicalized Yellow Vests."

He said some messages invoked Halloween while calling for "revolution" and "insurrection," describing them as incitements to serious public disorder and warning that the gatherings would be banned.

In recent days, the word "purge" has been circulating across social media platforms, a reference to the dystopian film franchise which depicts a world where all crime is legalized for a 12-hour period each year.

"At Halloween, the rules remain the same!" warned the Paris police on X, reminding people that concealing one's face in public is punishable by a €150 ($170) fine, while carrying a weapon, even a fake one, can carry a sentence of up to three years in prison and a €45,000 ($50,398) fine.

The French protests began in late September, led by high school students demanding improvements to deteriorating school buildings, teacher shortages and a lack of resources, as well as changes to the university admissions system.

The protests then morphed into something bigger, with the Yellow Vests, which began as a movement against soaring fuel prices, among those taking to the streets.

The images of violence and looting from the October 17 protests are still haunting French officials. That day, more than 550,000 people took to the streets across France, according to the Interior Ministry, more than 3,000 shops were attacked or looted, with some destroyed and over 2,700 people were arrested.

Asked about the students injured during the protests, President Emmanuel Macron described the violence as a "collective failure."

"I think no high school student started pushing for their demands expecting to suffer such terrible consequences. And I don't know a single police officer who signed up to find themselves caught up in such terrible and violent moments either," he told Youtuber Hugo Travers.

Saturday's demonstration comes ahead of November 5, when all eyes will be on a nationwide strike and mobilization called by the inter-union coalition over rising living costs.

articles.title: Alder Hey hospital admits responsibility for Mold girl's death
articles.summary: Eleanor Aldred-Owen died after surgery because an abnormal scan was not flagged.
articles.body:
A hospital trust has taken full responsibility for 24 failures that led to the death of a 21-month-old.

Eleanor Hazel Aldred-Owen died at Liverpool's Alder Hey Hospital on 2 October 2023 - a coroner concluded she died as a result of misadventure, contributed to by neglect.

She had routine surgery for craniosynostosis , a birth defect affecting the skull, but an abnormal chest X-ray was not flagged.

Eleanor suffered a cardiac arrest and unsurvivable brain injury and died in her parents' arms.

Her family, from Mold, Flintshire, said they have lived with "unbearable" guilt and trauma ever since.

Alder Hey Children's Hospital NHS Foundation Trust said her "tragic" death "should not have happened".

Eleanor's dad Chaz said: "Not knowing how or why Eleanor died was the key factors and what kept us going was justice for her.

"The real victory is making sure what happened to Eleanor doesn't happen to anyone else. No other family or child will have to go through what we have."

He added both he and his wife Rachel were "fairly certain it was neglectful" but did not realise the extent and were "at the mercy of what Alder Hey were telling us".

"They said it was breach of duty and not gross neglect and it took a long time for the trust to admit that."

He said the trust "being compelled to admit gross neglect" was the hardest thing.

Eleanor had routine surgery for craniosynostosis on 29 September 2023 and it went as planned, apart from the accidental removal of the breathing tube used during anaesthetic, which was replaced by the anaesthetist and the procedure continued.

During recovery, Eleanor had a raised heart rate and needed oxygen, and a decision was made to start AIRVO, a type of high-flow humidified oxygen, which was undocumented and not prescribed in accordance with trust's guidelines.

After her operation, Eleanor developed a collapsed lung as a result of surgery.

A radiographer failed to flag her abnormal chest X-ray to anyone on the ward, and the doctor did not review it immediately because she was in A&E reviewing another child.

Eleanor had a cardiac arrest before the collapsed lung was identified and treated, causing an unsurvivable brain injury.

An investigation found there were 24 failures in care that resulted in her death.

These included failure to correctly calculate her Paediatric Early Warning System score on several occasions, which would have led to a much earlier medical review and chest X-ray.

In a statement, her family said: "Eleanor's death was preventable and should not have happened.

"As parents, the guilt is unbearable, even though we know Eleanor was failed by the trust and not by us. We are irreversibly changed as people.

"We don't just constantly grieve for her, we grieve for the people we used to be when our daughter was here."

They said they recognised the changes the trust has implemented following Eleanor's death, but these had to be "used properly, kept under review and make care safer for other children".

Chaz said two post-operative procedures had been brought in to Alder Hey and named after Eleanor and changes the hospital had put in place was Eleanor's legacy and something he and his wife could be proud of.

Lynda Reynolds, the family's solicitor and partner at Hugh James, said it was "an unimaginably tragic case".

"Eleanor's parents placed their trust in Alder Hey Children's Hospital to care for their daughter and were let down.

"For Eleanor's family, the trust's acceptance of responsibility and public apology are important, but this follows a long and painful process.

"We hope that the changes the trust have implemented continue to make care safer for other children."

Alder Hey Children's NHS Foundation Trust said "the shocking loss of Eleanor has left a permanent mark on us all".

"We are heartbroken that we failed Eleanor and her family and we want to make sure that such a tragedy does not happen again."

It added that the missed opportunities, including a failure to escalate grossly abnormal X-ray findings, led it to introduce a clear escalation process within the radiology department for grossly abnormal and time-critical findings.

The trust accepted full responsibility for these failures and said it was profoundly sorry they resulted in Eleanor's death.

Chaz said he does not want Eleanor to be forgotten and to be remembered for the person she was, not how she died.

"She was happy, strong and funny. She loved music and water. She loved us and we loved her."

articles.body: Kristen Wiig has relisted a modernist house in Pasadena just four months after purchasing it for $5.5 million. The property, set among mature oak and sycamore trees in Los Angeles’ San Rafael neighbourhood, combines California modernism with traditional Japanese architectural influences. Designed in 1965 by architects Ainsworth, Angel & McClellan, the house features redwood-lined interiors, travertine floors and expansive glass walls. Landscape architect Kenneth S. Nakaba designed the surrounding gardens, which extend across almost half an acre. According to The Spaces, Wiig initially returned the property to the market with an $800,000 markup.Kristen Wiig’s Pasadena house combines California modernism with Japanese designThe 1965 residence reflects a blend of California modernism and traditional Japanese architecture. Designed by Ainsworth, Angel & McClellan, the house sits within a secluded, tree-filled setting in San Rafael. Its interiors feature redwood-lined spaces, travertine flooring, original wood-panelled ceilings and built-in joinery. A raised-hearth fireplace preserves another distinctive architectural feature, while expansive windows bring views of the surrounding landscape into the living areas. The design maintains a close relationship between the interior and the outdoors, with a wraparound deck extending from the main living spaces.A suspended walkway leads into the three-level modernist residenceAccess to the house begins with a suspended walkway that passes through the surrounding tree canopy before reaching the entrance. Inside, the living spaces unfold across three levels, with large windows framing the mature vegetation outside. The main living areas open onto a wraparound deck, reinforcing the connection between the house and its landscaped surroundings. The property also includes a primary suite in its own private wing, complete with a sitting area and a bathroom illuminated by a skylight. These features, alongside the preserved wood ceilings and built-in furnishings, contribute to the residence’s distinctive mid-century character.Kenneth S Nakaba’s gardens include a swimming pool and separate guest quartersThe grounds were designed by landscape architect Kenneth S Nakaba and occupy almost half an acre of densely planted land. Winding garden paths pass through the vegetation, while a freeform swimming pool and an inset spa provide additional outdoor amenities. The property also has separate guest accommodation, comprising a living room, dining area, kitchen and bedroom. This arrangement gives the residence spaces for visitors beyond the main house, while the landscaped grounds provide a secluded setting beneath the mature trees. The combination of gardens, pool and independent guest quarters adds to the property’s range of indoor and outdoor living spaces.Kristen Wiig’s Pasadena home returns to the market after four monthsWiig bought the Pasadena house for $5.5 million in February 2026 and initially listed it for $6.3 million in May, according to The Spaces and Robb Report. The initial asking price represented an $800,000 increase over her purchase price. The property was marketed through Maisonre and Christie’s International Real Estate. However, subsequent coverage by Robb Report and Mansion Global reported that the asking price had been reduced after the initial listing. The price change highlights the distinction between the amount a seller hopes to receive and the eventual sale price. articles.title: A Canadian publisher once had 25 million Facebook followers and submitted more than 500,000 ads before Meta shut down its pages in 2020; a US appeals court has now upheld dismissal of its conversion claim
articles.summary: Losing access to a social media account can mean losing years of work, an established audience and an important source of business.
articles.body: Losing access to a social media account can mean losing years of work, an established audience and an important source of business. That was the situation faced by a Canadian online publisher whose Facebook pages once attracted around 25 million followers. The company had submitted more than 500,000 advertisements to Meta over the years, but thousands were rejected for violating advertising policies. In October 2020, Meta permanently shut down its Facebook pages, ending a relationship that had lasted more than a decade. The publisher took the company to court, arguing that the closure had interfered with its business and property rights.In a ruling dated October 30, 2026, in Shared Partnership v. Meta Platforms, Inc. (No. 25-2612), the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit upheld the dismissal of the publisher's conversion claim. According to the judgment available on the Ninth Circuit's website, the three-judge panel found that Meta was protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act because removing the company's Facebook pages was part of its role as a publisher. The court also rejected the argument that presenting the dispute as a contractual violation could take it outside that legal protection.How the publisher built its Facebook audienceShared Partnership is a Canadian company that creates and publishes online content. For more than ten years, it operated several Facebook pages and used Meta's self-service advertising platform to attract visitors to its website and social media accounts. Its business model relied on eye-catching and provocative advertisements designed to generate clicks. The company's employees acknowledged that some of its advertising methods involved what they described as misleading clickbait and questionable promotional material.At its peak, Shared had approximately 25 million Facebook followers. Over the years, it submitted more than 500,000 advertisements to Meta for review. Although most were accepted, the platform rejected more than 18,000 advertisements for various policy violations. These included advertisements containing sensational or adult material, images focusing excessively on particular body parts, and promotions involving products or services considered deceptive or misleading.One rejected advertisement featured images of damaged cars and actor Luke Wilson alongside claims about a horrific fatal car crash. Facebook rejected it because its policies did not allow shocking or sensational content, including images depicting violence. The company was unhappy with the explanations provided for rejected advertisements. Its chief executive, Jordan Nabigon, believed Meta should provide customised feedback that would help the publisher edit advertisements and bring them into compliance. Despite the repeated rejections, Shared continued advertising on Facebook until the relationship ended.Meta shuts down the pages in 2020In October 2020, Meta cancelled Shared's Facebook pages, citing repeated violations of its terms and policies. The publisher considered the decision devastating for its business. It argued that losing its Facebook presence meant losing access to an audience it had spent years building. Shared subsequently sued Meta in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Among its claims was conversion, a legal claim generally involving the wrongful interference with another party's personal property.The company argued that it had an exclusive property interest in its Facebook pages and that Meta had unlawfully interfered with those rights by removing them. However, the district court dismissed the conversion claim, finding that Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act protected Meta from liability for decisions involving the publication or removal of third-party content. Shared appealed the decision to the Ninth Circuit.Why the publisher argued Meta breached its agreementBefore the appeals court, Shared argued that its case was not simply about Meta's decision to remove content. It recast its conversion theory as a breach-of-contract argument, relying on Facebook's Terms of Service. The company maintained that Meta could suspend or permanently disable an account only when a user had clearly, seriously or repeatedly violated its terms or policies.Shared argued that it had not committed the violations necessary to justify the closure. It also referred to an earlier Ninth Circuit decision, Calise v. Meta Platforms, which recognised that certain contractual claims could fall outside Section 230 protection when they involved obligations separate from a platform's publishing activities. The appeals court rejected this argument, finding that the relevant terms did not establish the separate contractual promise Shared was asserting.Court explains why Section 230 protects MetaThe appeals court rejected Shared's arguments on the conversion claim. Writing for the panel, Circuit Judge Kenneth Lee explained that Section 230 protects online platforms when they act as publishers or speakers of content supplied by others. The judges noted that publishing also includes deciding whether to remove content or prevent it from appearing on a platform. Therefore, Meta's decision to unpublish Shared's Facebook pages fell within its editorial responsibilities. The judges distinguished the case from Calise, where the contractual promise involved Meta's commitment to combat deceptive advertising, rather than its general editorial authority over content.The Ninth Circuit ultimately affirmed the dismissal of Shared's conversion claim, leaving the lower court's decision intact. The October 30 ruling reinforces that online platforms can rely on Section 230 protection when deciding whether to remove users and their content, even when those decisions have significant consequences for a publisher's business.You use AI every day. articles.title: Forgotten Flavours Of Tribal Kitchens: Beyond Millets, How The Mainstream Offers Taste Of Only A Fraction Of The Culinary Traditions Of MP & CG Communities
articles.summary: Explore Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh tribal cuisines beyond millets—seasonal greens, mahua, meat, fish, preservation methods, and diverse regional recipes.
articles.body: Bhopal/Raipur: Long before millets became a restaurant trend and political flavour of the day, lesser millet grains such as kodo and kutki were staples in tribal homes across Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. But they were only part of a wider food tradition that included seasonal greens, mushrooms, mahua flowers, fish and meat.Food historian and culinary scholar Pushpesh Pant believes the growing interest in tribal cuisine often captures only a fraction of these traditions.“Tribal food in the mainstream has not developed. It is slowly dying down,” Pant said, arguing that its revival often amounts to selective repackaging rather than recovery of knowledge.Flatbread Of DiversityOne cuisine does not exist. The food traditions of tribes such as the Gonds, Baigas, Bhils, Korkus, Murias and Oraons differ according to geography, available ingredients and household practices. Even within a community, recipes can vary. “All tribes cannot be found on the same page,” Pant told TOI.In MP, Bhil food traditions include dal paniya, made by wrapping maize-flour dough in leaves and cooking it over a fire. For botanist and anthropologist Madhu Ramnath, who has spent years working with Bastar’s Durwa community, gathering food is itself a form of knowledge. “Food collection gives them their particular identity,” he said.Unfinished Cookbook?The millet story too is incomplete. Kodo and kutki, two nutrient-dense neglected millet grains native to India, have long been part of central India’s food and farming systems. They may be cooked whole, made into porridge or ground into flour, depending on local practices. In MP, kutki is also used in sweet preparations such as kheer, while millet-based gruels and drinks have provided hearty refreshments during long days of work.Among the Kamar community in parts of Chhattisgarh’s Dhamtari and Gariaband, mandiyo, or finger millet, is used to prepare Mandiyo Pej, a non-alcoholic drink.Their preparation relies on knowledge of proportions, cooking time and texture, often passed down generations through observation rather than written recipes.The Missing PlateMeat, poultry and fish feature in the traditional diets of several tribal communities, although usage varies by region and household. In parts of Bastar, fish is eaten fresh or preserved for later use. Suksi, or dried fish, is one example of a preserved ingredient used in preparations.Drying, wherein the fish is methodically cleaned, salted and left in the sun to make it crisp, and smoking extend the shelf life of food. In Bastar, households have traditionally dried seasonal vegetables. An account from Gudiyapadar village documents the drying of corn, mushrooms, bitter gourds and tomatoes.Sukka Markam, a Bastar resident, also described roasting chicken over a fire before storing it, with the dried meat reportedly lasting three to four months. Such methods helped households retain seasonal foods through the year, particularly when heavy rain made remote villages difficult to access or seasonal vegetables were unavailable in weekly markets. So, presenting tribal food mainly through vegetarian dishes can leave out important chapters.The Chutney Of Books & FilmsOne of the best-known preparations associated with Bastar, featured in books and films, is chaprah chutney, made from red weaver ants and their eggs.Such foods need to be documented in their local context, without being reduced to curiosities or sensationalised for outside audiences. Their culinary significance should also be distinguished from potential medicinal claims.Tree Of Life Sustains KitchensFor Adivasi communities, mahua’s cultural significance goes well beyond the beverage made from its flowers. Its flowers, fruit, seeds, branches and other parts sustain dishes and livelihoods.Describing its place in community life, Ram Manjhi said, “The entire mahua tree... from its roots to its dry branches, flowers and fruit, even its shade, is embedded in their lives. Their culture can’t be understood without it.”Preserving More Than RecipesResearch in Chhattisgarh’s Kamar villages has recorded that some younger people find traditional preparations less appealing or time-consuming.For Pant, revival should not mean recreating an imagined past or fitting different communities into a single menu. “There is no harm in reviving a lost way of life which restores pride for tribals and creates employment opportunities for them,” he said.But the culinary heritage of Adivasi communities in MP and Chhattisgarh cannot be represented by a few celebrated dishes or ingredients. articles.title: King to address slavery during Commonwealth speech in Antigua on final leg of Caribbean tour
articles.summary: The King will deliver a speech to Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting as he concludes his nine-day Caribbean tour.
articles.body:
King Charles is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade, during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.

The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech which will touch on the issue.

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.

It is understood that the Palace had been told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of the comments.

The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.

Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.

The King will make his speech on Tuesday at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit," a Palace spokesperson said.

"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow, and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."

When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to "the UK Government's position".

The Caribbean tour has again thrust King Charles into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.

Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology are a matter for government, not the Palace.

"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to 'bat for Britain', the Realms and wider Commonwealth."

In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation" , and that Britain "must face up to the past".

His pledge to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by King Charles, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.

"Institutions are under strain across the globe," said a Palace spokesperson. "The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."

The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".

Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua, and they will attend a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island.

In addition, his son, Prince Harry, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, in August.

Asked if the King was confident that his approach to family matters has been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise: "Yes. That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done", a senior aide told the BBC.

On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."

The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory."

In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.
